output.headline: Leaked figures reveal scale of England's ADHD and autism diagnosis surge
output.bodyHtml:
A major government-commissioned review into England’s rising demand for mental health, ADHD and autism support has been postponed until early next month. It comes as NHS bodies impose a minimum wait of at least two years on people with suspected ADHD or autism before they can be assessed, as they struggle to meet soaring demand for diagnoses of neurodiversity.

Four NHS integrated care boards (ICBs) covering large regions of England have adopted the approach because they cannot afford the cost of the number of assessments that people are seeking.

Patient groups are warning that the ‘scandalous’ delays such policies involve may damage children’s chances of succeeding at school, deny people the help they need to manage their lives, and increase the risk of suicide. The charity ADHD UK denounced minimum waits as ‘heartless and dangerous’.

In all, 15 ICBs, which between them cover 19 million people, have brought in various ways of rationing assessments for ADHD and autism to try to balance their books. These include limiting the number of assessments the ICBs will pay for in any given year and using ‘clinical prioritisation’ criteria to restrict assessment to those with the most serious signs of neurodiversity.

The findings come as the government prepares to publish a major review into the colossal rise in diagnoses of mental illness, as well as ADHD and autism, in recent years. Commissioned last year by Wes Streeting, the then health secretary, the review was ordered amid concern that the weight of requests for assessment, diagnosis and care was overwhelming the health service’s ability to meet demand.

The 700-page report of the review, led by Prof Peter Fonagy, was due to be published on Thursday but was unexpectedly postponed until early next month.

Sources familiar with the document told the Guardian that it painted a detailed picture of how the fast-rising demand for help with mental illness conditions, ADHD and autism has left those affected struggling to get rapid access to NHS care and increasingly reliant on private providers.

Fonagy’s report raises serious concerns about the sector, especially about the consistency and quality of the assessments it provides and the fact that there are ‘financial incentives associated with assessment activity’.

It also lays bare the scale of the challenge that the increasing number of diagnoses of mental illness, ADHD and autism pose for the NHS, as well as schools, employers and families, by highlighting up to 24-fold rises in the prevalence of neurodiversity in boys since 2000.

It reveals that the percentage of seven- to 18-year-old boys with autism rose from 0.2 per cent in 2000 to 4.7 per cent in 2025. Prevalence among boys aged six to 11 rose from 0.4 per cent to 6.3 per cent over the same period – a 16-fold jump.

Similarly, the percentage of seven to 18-year-old boys diagnosed with ADHD rose from 0.4 per cent to 5.1 per cent between 2000 and 2025 – an almost 13-fold leap – and from 0.7 per cent to 3.8 per cent – up five-fold – among boys aged six to 11, according to figures provided by the Clinical Practice Research Datalink.

Many patients already exercise their legal right to choose non-NHS care, given the NHS’s own limited capacity to carry out the assessments – private clinics now undertake half of NHS-funded assessments for ADHD and a third of those for autism. But ‘minimum waits’ after referral by a GP mean people in the areas affected can no longer seek an assessment from a private provider.

Such curbs by the NHS are likely to force those who can afford it to pay a private provider for an assessment for themselves or their child, which can cost several thousand pounds. They are being implemented at a time when there are 960,000 people in England waiting for an ADHD assessment and another 295,000 awaiting one for autism.

West Yorkshire NHS integrated care board has introduced a minimum waiting time of two years from referral for anyone seeking an ADHD or autism assessment with an independent provider. That was in response to its bill for such assessments soaring from £7m in 2023-24 to £21m last year, it said.

The West Yorkshire ICB’s decision applies to the 2.4 million people for whom it commissions and pays for care in Leeds, Bradford, Kirklees, Calderdale and Wakefield. Its area includes the constituency of Pontefract, Castleford and Knottingley – the parliamentary seat of the health secretary Yvette Cooper.

Private providers that the North East and North Cumbria ICB funds to assess people ‘are working to an approximately 78-week minimum waiting time for an initial assessment’, it says.

Somerset ICB is operating a minimum wait of 52 weeks, while the equivalent in Devon is a lot lower, at 14 weeks. Kent and Medway ICB has also decided to impose a minimum wait.

This month, the ICB covering Hampshire and the Isle of Wight restricted assessment for ADHD and autism to those patients who meet its priority criteria.

‘It’s scandalous that any NHS body should impose a two-year minimum wait for ADHD and autism assessments,’ said Henry Shelford, the chief executive of ADHD UK.

‘This is the health service denying people care they need, and care that is available, and slamming the door shut on people who need an assessment of their symptoms to give them a diagnosis and unlock essential care that helps people hold down jobs, stay in education and stay out of crisis services.

‘A minimum wait is heartless and dangerous. It is institutionalised cruelty.’

A spokesperson for Finally Seen, which tracks NHS restrictions on the right to choose, said: ‘A two-year minimum wait is not a waiting list. It is a locked door with a date on it.

‘The right to choose still exists on paper. In practice it is being rationed by the calendar, which is a blunt and bleak way to treat a legal right.’

Rebecca Gray, the director of the NHS Alliance’s mental health network, said local NHS leaders were ‘keenly aware of the deep frustration caused by long delays and are doing all they can to address them.

‘But the need to balance budgets and the pressures of soaring demand have – in some places – led to “minimum waits” or even the closure of some waiting lists.

‘The current situation is unsustainable and delivers a bad deal for patients and taxpayers.’

The British Medical Journal recently revealed that 17 of the 36 ICBs had introduced minimum waits of 12 to 16 weeks before patients could have a new hip or knee fitted or cataract removed, even though the NHS is meant to give 92 per cent of patients planned hospital care within 18 weeks.

Mel Merritt, the head of policy and influencing at the National Autistic Society, said: ‘Restricting access to autism assessments denies people support because, while it shouldn’t be the case, a diagnosis is needed to get help. For children, this can mean years of wasted school while they wait for an assessment and further waits to get a plan for support and adjustments to be put into place.

‘A diagnosis doesn’t only confirm if people are autistic or not, but also their needs and what adjustments could make a massive difference to being able to participate and enjoy life. Longer waiting times and restricting access to assessments will only worsen challenges for autistic people, pushing them into crisis and increasing the number of people with urgent needs.’

Related: ‘Her mental health deteriorated’: family forced to wait years for autism diagnosis

The Independent Healthcare Providers Network, which represents many independent assessment services, urged the NHS to let private clinics offer as many appointments as were available.

Sean Phillips, its head of policy, said: ‘For someone struggling with suspected ADHD or autism, those extra months or years without diagnosis and support can have a profound impact on their mental health, education, work and family life.

‘With more than a million people already waiting, we should be using all available capacity to get people the support and treatment they need as well as ensuring that their legal right to choose the best provider for them is being upheld.’
output.standfirst: Sources close to a postponed government review reveal the scale of England's ADHD and autism diagnosis surge, as four NHS bodies impose a two-year wait for assessments branded 'scandalous' by patient groups.
output.progress: The government commissioned a review into soaring demand for ADHD, autism and mental health assessments; its publication has been postponed until early next month.

output.headline: Xi Jinping and Trump chart course for deeper US-China cooperation
output.bodyHtml:
Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the ‘Thucydides trap’ that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan.

At the start of his summit meeting with Donald Trump in the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could steer the two competing superpowers away from future military conflict and on to a road of mutual gain.

Rather than confrontation, conditions for ‘achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand’ and should be the goal, Xi said, citing Trump’s political catchphrase.

Related: Trump swoons over strongman soulmate Xi – are you feeling jealous, Vladimir?

‘We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,’ said Xi, with Trump looking on.

‘We should coexist in peace. China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.’

With such conditions in place, Xi said, ‘the Thucydides trap can be overcome’, referring to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power.

Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it.

His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other.

Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was president.

‘President Xi and Madame Peng arrive at an important moment for America, the 250th anniversary of our founding,’ he said.

Trump said he had forged ‘a truly great friendship’ with Xi. ‘President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,’ he said. ‘Our teams have been working to encourage a more balances trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.’

He said the current visit would include discussion over security, technology and AI – which he called ‘super intelligence’, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday.

Xi also extolled his personal relationship with his American counterpart, saying: ‘President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.’

Addressing Trump directly, he said: ‘During your visit to China this year, we agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability. I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course towards the future.’

The White House welcome ceremony came after Trump had taken the unusual step of going to Andrews air force base in Maryland the evening before to greet the Chinese leader and his wife on the tarmac.

Much of the same pageantry was repeated in Thursday’s ceremony, with both countries’ national anthems being played. Trump was flanked by his wife, Melania, while members of his cabinet and senior aides – including Natalie Harp, Trump’s dedicated assistant nicknamed ‘the human printer’ by fellow staffers – looked on.

Trump and Xi held bilateral talks after the ceremony and the welcoming speeches.

Later on Thursday, Trump hosted Xi at the White House for a state dinner. Notable invited guests from the tech world included Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Apple chair Tim Cook, SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

Trump gestured to the titans of the industry in his remarks to the dinner, recounting when Chinese diplomats first arrived in the US 158 years ago, meeting American intellectuals like Henry David Thoreau and prominent political figures.

‘Tonight, we revive the spirit of that first encounter here on American soil as we are joined by some of the top leaders in business, culture and government from our own time,’ he said. ‘On one side, China draws on thousands of years of history and tradition from Sun Tzu to Sun Yat-sen. For Americans, we inherit a legacy of faith from Jerusalem to Rome, democracy of ancient Athens, the triumphs of Sparta and the freedom proclaimed in Philadelphia 250 years ago.’

Trump also touted his relationship with the Chinese leader.

‘President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better,’ he said.

Xi also addressed the dinner, saying talks with Trump during the visit had yielded ‘common understanding on many issues’, and suggesting the US and China find a new approach to working together.

‘China and the United States must act as responsible major countries,’ he said.

Despite the harmonious tone adopted by both leaders, analysts have voiced scepticism about the possibility of longstanding stable arrangements being arrived at over a host of issues.

In the race for AI, the US has placed strict export controls on microchips, semiconductors, software and chip-making equipment in a bid to slow China’s development.

A truce agreed between Trump and Xi in South Korea last year aimed at keeping tariffs lower had been due to expire in November but has now been extended until February, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent said.

Analysts believe the extension suggests Trump continues to be dissatisfied with Xi’s concession offers on trade and wants to keep the pressure on in the hope of getting a better deal if the two meet again at the G20 summit scheduled to be held in Miami in December.

Despite the trade war between the two countries, Chinese imports have continued to surge into the US. China is on course to run a $1tn trade deficit for the second year running.

Uwa Ede-Osifo contributed reporting

  • The headline and text of this article were amended on 24 September 2026 to correct a misspelling of Xi Jinping.
output.standfirst: Xi Jinping and Donald Trump pledged deeper dialogue and peaceful coexistence, as the two countries extended their tariff truce to February, but analysts remain sceptical that lasting stability can be reached between the rival powers.
output.progress: Xi Jinping has invited 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges as both leaders pledge closer dialogue.

output.headline: Livestreamed footage leads police to charge Daniel Thomas over Channel dinghy
output.bodyHtml:
Police and prosecutors acted on Daniel Thomas’s own livestreamed footage to charge the far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist with criminal damage and with failing to disclose his phone pin to police, after an incident in the Channel on Tuesday in which he allegedly slashed a dinghy while a French rescuer was on board.

Thomas, 37, of no fixed abode, has been charged with one count of criminal damage and with an offence under section 53 of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (Ripa), for allegedly failing to comply with a notice to disclose a phone pin to police.

He has been remanded in custody and is due to appear via videolink at Basingstoke magistrates court on Friday.

Chris Derrick, of the Crown Prosecution Service, said: ‘The CPS has decided to prosecute Daniel Thomas following an investigation by Hampshire constabulary into an incident on Tuesday 22 September.’

‘Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue criminal proceedings.’

‘We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial.’

Hundreds of people gathered outside Basingstoke investigation centre, where Thomas was believed to be held, on Thursday evening.

They included scores of mainly men dressed all in black, though the vast majority were not covering their faces. One person said he had come from Manchester to take part in the protest.

Some chanted: ‘Free DT’ and ‘Oh, Danny, Danny’. One person had brought a sign reading: ‘Get Danny out.’

Extra police were drafted in from forces as far away as Kent, and a police drone hovered above the protest.

Thomas’s livestreamed footage appeared to show him approaching one of the dinghies, which was empty, shouting: ‘Let’s get rid of that boat.’ After the rescue worker got onboard, Thomas shouted: ‘Get off the boat. You’ve got time to get off the boat.’ His footage shows his boat speeding away before the rescue worker climbed back on to a larger boat.

Thomas, who goes by the name Danny Tommo, had spent the afternoon in a boat, filming himself as he tracked two dinghies carrying asylum seekers from France to the UK. The livestreamed footage was watched by more than 200,000 people.

A longtime associate of fellow far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, AKA Tommy Robinson, Thomas this summer gathered dozens of nationalist protest groups under the umbrella anti-immigration movement Patriot Platform.

Thomas repeatedly told his followers they should march silently, without violence, and avoid doing anything that could lead to arrests. The organisation, Patriot Platform, was behind marches this month in Dover and Portsmouth, when masked men in black gathered and protested over immigration and asylum policy.

Thomas apparently managed to film and upload footage of his own arrest before police were able to stop him. On Wednesday night a 56-second clip was uploaded to his YouTube platform showing a police officer telling him he was being arrested on suspicion of criminal damage and ‘recklessly endangering someone’s life’.

Thomas said: ‘I understand. I knew this was coming.’

The latest Home Office figures put renewed focus on the government’s handling of small boat arrivals in the UK. A government spokesperson said: ‘Our progress this year in tackling small boats is indisputable, with crossings down by 42 per cent and the lowest recorded over the summer months since 2020.’

Responding to the figures, the government said it would ‘push further and harder’ to crack down on the people organising the crossings, after the Home Office recorded 781 arrivals in 10 boats on Wednesday, the highest number for a single day so far this year.

‘But this week’s events show that while the peaks we are seeing are far below those of previous years, we need to push further and harder in order to eradicate this vile trade.’

Wednesday’s arrivals take the provisional total for Channel crossings for the year so far to 18,565. Home Office data indicates this is down 42 per cent on this time last year (32,188) and 26 per cent below the figure at this stage in 2024 (25,165).

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has ordered an urgent review by Border Security Command, describing the failure to intercept the two boats as ‘not acceptable’.

Most small boats carrying asylum seekers to the UK are escorted to shore by rescue services or Border Force vessels, and no unescorted small boat had been recorded since 6 September 2025 before ministers this week became concerned by two uncontrolled landings from the Channel in two days.

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, said: ‘You can’t stop everything all of the time,’ after 21 people were detained when a boat evaded Border Force to reach the beach of Samphire Hoe in Dover on Wednesday. Another dinghy made an uncontrolled landing in Folkestone on Monday morning.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Powell said: ‘Of course, it’s a concern. That’s why the home secretary has demanded and ordered this urgent review, because this is not what we want to see. This is not acceptable.’

A court jailed a 42-year-old man on Thursday after he threw a plastic bottle at a police line and swore at officers during an anti-migrant protest in Portsmouth.

Del Somerville, of Paulsgrove, was sentenced at Portsmouth crown court to two years in prison, having previously pleaded guilty to the charge of violent disorder. He is the first to be sentenced over violence that erupted after the arrival of a small boat in the Hampshire city on 6 September.

Judge Daniel Sawyer told him his sentence would act as a deterrent to others after subsequent protests in the area. Describing Somerville as a ‘thug’, he told the defendant: ‘Police officers dedicate their lives to the protection of the public regardless of their own views, the very least they can expect is that those who engage in protests treat them with respect and the courts punish those who assault them.’
output.standfirst: Footage he livestreamed helped police charge Daniel Thomas, 37, with criminal damage over a Channel dinghy allegedly slashed while a French rescue worker was aboard. He also faces a charge for withholding his phone pin.
output.progress: The Crown Prosecution Service has charged Daniel Thomas with criminal damage after Hampshire police investigated Tuesday's Channel incident.

output.headline: Protesters and diplomats challenge Netanyahu's defiant Gaza speech at the UN
output.bodyHtml:
Dozens of delegates, inspired by a Palestinian call, walked out of the General Assembly Hall of the UN headquarters as Netanyahu took the stage, leading a speaker to pound his gavel and announce: ‘I’m calling for order in the hall.’

Palestinian representatives organising diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech said they wanted to ‘send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end’.

‘If there are any other moral cowards in the audience, I urge them to walk out,’ Netanyahu said before launching into his prepared remarks.

Benjamin Netanyahu delivered an inflammatory address to the United Nations on Thursday, decrying what he said was a global anti-Jewish conspiracy and swatting aside criticism of Israel’s war in Gaza, as he faces down international isolation and a fight for political survival in upcoming elections in Israel.

As planned protests erupted on the streets of New York City, Netanyahu took aim at critics of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, the international media, regional leaders such as Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, the leftwing commentator Hasan Piker and the New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani in an address that doubled as a stump speech to ignite his rightwing base for the elections.

Invoking his late brother Yonatan Netanyahu, a commando killed in a 1976 raid to free Israeli hostages from a hijacked airliner in Entebbe, Uganda, he repeated the lines: ‘We are going to win. We have no other choice.’

The speech revealed little new in terms of Israeli policy over the war in Gaza, militant settler violence in the West Bank, or Israel’s plans to end other regional conflicts including its joint war with the United States against Iran.

But he argued that the world faced an existential threat from Iran, suggesting that several missiles from Tehran could have destroyed the UN, and cited quiet support from world leaders for Israel’s actions that could not be aired in public.

‘Devastating Iran’s nuclear facilities was … very hard to do,’ he said of launching joint US-Israeli strikes in February. ‘But for me, it was one of the easiest decisions I’ve ever had to make as prime minister. Because if we hadn’t done it, we’d all be dead.’

He branded Turkey’s Erdoğan as a ‘tyrant’ who ‘hosts Hamas terrorists’, decried Mamdani as the ‘antisemitic mayor of New York’ and declared that Israel’s war in Gaza is not genocide – ‘it’s the opposite of genocide’.

‘So, to all those spreading these lies about my country and about our brave soldiers, whether they sit in this hall or in the office of the antisemitic mayor of New York, I say this: shame on you!’ he said.

Netanyahu delivered the controversial address to the United Nations on Thursday just hours after Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas said his delegation was ‘unlawfully’ denied visas by the Trump administration to attend the meeting of world leaders.

Related: Netanyahu’s speech at UN spurs protests in New York City: ‘Let Gaza live’

In a video address from Ramallah, broadcast in the General Assembly Hall, Abbas condemned Israel’s policies in Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem as a ‘malicious colonial plan’ to establish a ‘“Greater Israel” and erase the Palestinian presence’.

Citing the humanitarian crisis in Gaza and the violent expansion of settlements in the West Bank, Abbas said that the Israeli government ‘now threatens the very life and existence of the Palestinian people in their homeland’.

‘Do not allow another Nakba and further massacres like those of 1948 to continue taking place,’ he added, referring to the expulsion of Palestinians upon the founding of Israel.

For the second year in a row, the US state department denied visas to Abbas and the Palestinian Authority delegation, arguing that they had failed to live up to their commitments to seek peace with Israel.

‘As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,’ the state department said last week in a statement.

In his speech, Abbas said his delegation ‘[rejects] these unlawful punitive measures, as well as the accusations and justifications on which they were based’.

He said: ‘Preventing the Palestinian delegation from reaching United Nations headquarters is inconsistent with the obligations of the United States as the host country.’

As he spoke, protests were forming on the streets of New York near the United Nations headquarters in advance of Netanyahu’s arrival.

Hundreds of demonstrators crowded into the street on Manhattan’s east side in midtown and held signs that said ‘End the Genocide’ and wore shirts reading ‘Fund people not bombs’. By the end of Netanyahu’s speech, more than 100 demonstrators, including several local elected officials, had been arrested by New York City police.

Earlier this summer, the mayor, Zohran Mamdani, had said that Netanyahu was ‘not welcome’ in New York, and said he was reviewing whether Netanyahu could be arrested by city police under an international criminal court warrant for his arrest.

He has since tempered that stance, saying this week that he wouldn’t attend the protests but promising to protect their ‘right to [protest] in this city’.

Netanyahu is not expected to meet Donald Trump, who is in Washington to host the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, nor with other senior US officials, as he faces growing international condemnation over his hardline stance. Netanyahu has said that he needs to return to Israel quickly because of the election campaign and the holiday of Sukkot, which begins on Friday.
output.standfirst: Hundreds of protesters and dozens of walkout delegates responded to Netanyahu’s inflammatory UN address, in which he attacked critics and branded mayor Zohran Mamdani ‘antisemitic’, after Mahmoud Abbas said his delegation was unlawfully denied US visas.
output.progress: Hundreds of protesters and dozens of UN delegates responded by demonstrating and walking out, while mayor Zohran Mamdani vowed to protect their right to protest.

output.headline: Farming leaders call for a long-term plan to secure Britain's food supply
output.bodyHtml:
Industry leaders have called on the government to protect homegrown produce in the interest of national security, after the UK's food and drink trade deficit rose to more than £21bn – the largest it has been since 2000 – in what they called a 'wake-up call'.

The gap between Britain's food and drink exports and imports has neared its highest level this century, with Brexit, war in the Middle East and US tariffs denting deliveries overseas while imports soared.

Tom Bradshaw, the president of the National Farmers' Union of England and Wales, said: 'These figures should be a wake-up call. At a time of growing geopolitical uncertainty, we cannot afford to take our food production capacity for granted.'

He said the widening trade deficit underlined the need for a long-term plan to support British production and recognise 'a simple truth that food security is national security'.

'The pressures facing farm businesses are immense, from rising costs and regulatory burdens to extreme weather and global market volatility,' said Bradshaw. 'If government is serious about food security, economic growth and national resilience, it must create the conditions that give businesses the confidence to invest, innovate and grow.'

The Food and Drink Federation (FDF), which represents hundreds of food and beverage producers, said pressures on manufacturers were 'significant and growing' as the cost of energy, ingredients, transport, packaging and labour continued to rise, and said changing regulation was adding to those pressures.

Karen Betts, the chief executive of the trade body, said: 'Our food and drink trade deficit is growing and is now the largest it's been in over 25 years. In a world beset by conflict and the ever-increasing impacts of climate change, this poses some stark questions about our food security.

'When the government then chooses to remove tariffs on, for example, biscuits imported from China, it's not surprising that they'll be sold more cheaply here than biscuits made in the UK.'

UK food and drink export volumes fell by more than a tenth (11.7 per cent) in the first half of 2026 to 4bn kg, only marginally above levels at the height of the Covid pandemic and in the aftermath of the 2001 foot-and-mouth disease outbreak, according to analysis by the FDF.

Exports to the EU continued to fall – down 0.9 per cent in value – amid the additional costs and complexity of trading since Brexit.

The FDF recorded an even larger fall in exports beyond the EU – down 6.9 per cent in value terms. That was partly driven by disruption in sales to the Middle East, with exports to the UAE down by almost a quarter as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran. The US's introduction of a 10 per cent import tariff hit cross-Atlantic sales by 16.5 per cent.

Food and drink imports were 19.1bn kg in the first half of this year, the second highest ever, only beaten by the same period last year. Imports from outside the EU are up more than a fifth since 2023 as restrictions have been eased through trade deals, particularly with Australia, which now sends 25 per cent more in value terms to the UK than a year ago, including meat, oils, vegetables and even whisky.

The suspension of tariffs on a range of manufactured foods, including chocolate and biscuits, this year as part of the former chancellor Rachel Reeves's package to ease the cost of living has also raised import levels. EU food producers, meanwhile, increased deliveries to the UK in value terms – up 0.8 per cent year-on-year – having recovered in volume terms since Brexit.
output.standfirst: Farming and food industry leaders are calling on the government to treat food security as national security, after the UK's food and drink trade deficit widened to more than £21bn, the largest since 2000.
output.progress: The National Farmers' Union and Food and Drink Federation are calling on the government to support British food production as a national security priority.

output.headline: Brazilian politicians across party lines defend democracy against Trump interference claims
output.bodyHtml:
Politicians from across Brazil's political spectrum have pushed back against alleged US interference in the country's presidential election, after Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's campaign accused Donald Trump of wanting to 'colonise' Brazil and capture its natural resources by meddling in next month's vote.

The accusation came in a televised campaign advert that was broadcast on Thursday by Lula's team amid growing fears over the impact alleged US interference could have on the vote.

The TV spot claimed the US president was trying to sway the election in favour of Lula's far-right adversary in the election, Flávio Bolsonaro, in order to advance Trump's interests in the South American nation.

'Flávio Bolsonaro is Trump's candidate and what Trump wants is to colonise Brazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust,' the female narrator tells viewers in the minute-long video.

The state department has denied claims the US is meddling in Brazil's election. 'Any insinuation of a "ploy" to undermine a democratic nation's election is a baseless lie,' it said last month in a statement.

Related: 'A coin flip': on the campaign trail as Brazil's far right edges back to power

Writing on X, Lula accused Bolsonaro of wanting to 'hand our natural resources over to the United States'.

'If it's up to him, Brazil will become a colony again,' the incumbent leftwing president added.

With just over a week to go until the 4 October first round vote, Lula and Bolsonaro are neck and neck in the polls. A second round run-off will be held on 25 October if no candidate secures more than half of the votes.

In recent weeks, there has been growing alarm – both in Brazil and overseas – about Washington's apparent attempts to influence the result, with a campaign of diplomatic and economic pressure, including 25 per cent tariffs on Brazilian imports.

Speaking at the UN general assembly in New York this week, Lula indirectly criticised the US' perceived meddling, telling delegates: 'We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people. Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians.'

Earlier this week, dozens of Democratic party congresspeople wrote to secretary of state, Marco Rubio, to denounce the Trump administration's 'apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine' Brazil's elections through what they called a 'sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilisation in Brazil'.

The narrator of Lula's campaign ad cited a series of recent media stories relating to alleged acts of US meddling.

They include reports about the alleged interference of Big Tech companies as well as a confidential document sent to electoral authorities by Brazil's intelligence agency warning of a 'critical level' of risk of US interference. The campaign video also highlighted recent claims about links between Bolsonaro's campaign and the conservative donor network Rockbridge, which was co-founded by Trump's vice-president JD Vance.

Éden Valadares, the communications secretary for Lula's Worker's party (PT), said the campaign ad was part of efforts to 'alert the Brazilian people' to the ideologically-driven US campaign. 'We don't believe it will work but nor will we sit back and do nothing,' Valadares said.

'President Lula has instructed us … to mobilise Brazilian society … [and] to react in the streets,' added Valadares, who said a nationwide series of events were being planned for this Sunday.

Fears over US meddling are not confined to the Brazilian left. This week, another of the right-wing candidates in Brazil's election, Renan Santos, also denounced Trump's behaviour and said he did not want Brazil to become a US vassal state. 'They want to interfere in Brazil's elections to secure satisfactory contracts involving rare earths,' Santos claimed in a social media video.

Recalling the US invasion of Venezuela in January, Santos added: 'I don't want to see Latin America become an American protectorate.'

In the letter sent to Rubio on Friday, the Democratic lawmakers wrote that 'rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy', the US was 'acting as an agent of interference and destabilisation – using diplomatic, economic and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country's democratic institutions, undermining confidence in Brazil's electoral process, and inflicting further damage on our relationship with a strategic US ally and trading partner'.

They asked Rubio if Trump's administration would commit to respecting Brazil's electoral process and requested a response by 1 October. The state department has not yet responded to a request for comment.

output.headline: Germany and Nordic allies back UK's inclusion in EU industry plan
output.bodyHtml:
Germany and Nordic countries are pushing for a broader EU definition of ‘Made in Europe’ that would include the UK, even as France leads a move to exclude Britain from the policy – a shift that could see British companies lose out in the race to supply European countries with low-carbon technologies and electric cars.

Germany wants a broader ‘Made with Europe’ policy that would include the UK and other allies. Germany’s economic affairs minister, Katherina Reiche, told her counterparts: ‘We must reduce unilateral and critical dependencies, but we must not isolate ourselves from the rest of the world. This means that partner countries must be included in the union-origin principle, in general and on the condition of reciprocity.’

This position gets broad support from Nordic countries, which traditionally favour open trade.

Sweden’s outgoing deputy prime minister, Ebba Busch, who leads on business policy, said ‘we always miss the Brits’. Sweden wanted ‘a good solution where there is balance, given that some European countries are not members of the European Union but still completely essential for a functioning European market’, she added.

The plans were raised by Andy Burnham when he met the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, on the sidelines of the UN general assembly earlier this week.

The policy, still under negotiation, aims to protect European companies from intense and ‘unfair’ state-subsidised competition from China. But the government fears British companies risk being collateral damage and resolving the issue has become one of Burnham’s top priorities for the EU-UK relationship.

One key EU proposal is the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), which would require authorities spending public money – awarding subsidies or public contracts – to favour European products in sectors such as renewable technologies and electric cars.

But there is an intense debate inside the EU on how to define ‘made in Europe’ and how far to include countries such as the UK, Canada and Japan.

Related: UK ‘losing up to £6.5bn a year in EU trade’ without post-Brexit product deal

At a meeting of EU industry ministers in Brussels on Thursday, France pushed for a narrow definition, starting with the EU27.

‘European taxpayers’ money should support [European] workers and European factories,’ the French industry minister, Sébastien Martin, told reporters.

Asked about the UK, he said: ‘The United Kingdom made a choice a few years ago to leave the European Union.

‘That doesn’t mean that we don’t discuss things or that we don’t trade, it doesn’t mean that there can’t be agreements in certain sectors, but fundamentally there are those who have chosen the European project and those who have decided to leave.’

France’s Europe minister, Benjamin Haddad, speaking in London, had few assurances to offer the Burnham government either.

Asked about the risks of pushing the EU’s like-minded trading partners away, Haddad said: ‘At the end of the day, if you are not part of the internal market and if you are not contributing to the financial capacity of the internal market, you don’t get the same kind of protection.’

The charged internal EU27 debate on Made in Europe raises questions about the timing of the EU-UK reset summit, which was postponed when Keir Starmer stood down as prime minister. Since Burnham took office, no date has been fixed for the talks which are meant to happen in 2026.

British officials expect the summit will take place in November, although an earlier 6 November date has been scratched out. By December the EU is expected to be embroiled in deeply difficult internal negotiations on the bloc’s next seven-year budget, which are likely to consume the political bandwidth of EU leaders.

EU insiders believe that a Made in Europe agreement is a top priority for the UK, but have cautioned this cannot happen before the union has finalised its own position.

One EU diplomat said it was a ‘big risk’ if the UK government were to insist on a deal at an autumn summit. ‘It puts [the UK] in a corner, because this [Made in Europe criteria] is a process that is very difficult for the EU27 [to agree internally].’

The Republic of Ireland, which is chairing EU ministerial negotiations, hopes for an agreement in December on the IAA, including the Made in Europe provisions, between the EU Council and the European parliament. ‘There are a divergence of views on the Industrial Accelerator Act, on European preference, on working with trusted partners and third countries,’ said Ireland’s enterprise minister, Peter Burke. ‘It is difficult, but we have a pathway in sight.’

Poland’s economic development minister, Michał Baranowski, said it was too early to say whether countries such as Switzerland, the UK, Japan, Australia and Canada would be in or out, adding: ‘All these countries are in the mix of the discussion.’

The UK, he said, should have clarity on its status when the EU act is passed, adding: ‘We are in the last stretch, but this last stretch might take a while.’

A UK government spokesperson said: ‘The UK is a close and trusted European partner, committed to our shared security and economic cooperation.

‘We will continue to engage with the EU on Made in Europe and work together, as like-minded partners, to boost growth and open up trade.’

output.headline: Ed Miliband meets Iran's foreign minister for the first time
output.bodyHtml:
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, met Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, in New York for the first time – also the first meeting between UK and Iranian ministers in a year – as Tehran pressed its case for the US to lift sanctions and end the war on all fronts.

It was also the first exchange between UK and Iranian ministers since the UK in July proscribed the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organisation, a move that has worsened the already sour relations between the two countries.

Miliband made clear that the UK was committed to freedom of navigation in the strait and wanted a diplomatic solution, also stressing support for Saudi Arabia, a UK ally in Yemen.

He warned Iran about its behaviour in the UK, including threats to Jewish communities, and called for the UK to be given consular access to the British couple sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment in Tehran.

Araghchi and the US’s special envoy Steve Witkoff also met earlier this week on the sidelines of the general assembly to discuss Iran’s terms for reopening the strait and the speed at which that may happen, as well as the time the US had been given to respond.

Related: Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk

Iran said it has told Donald Trump it is willing to open the strait of Hormuz in six days, and to start talks on its nuclear programme the day after, so long as the US lifts sanctions on Iran’s oil exports in return, ends the war on all fronts – including in Lebanon – and releases some of Iran’s frozen assets.

The proposal is designed to accelerate the steps first laid down in the memorandum of understanding signed by the US and Iran in June, particularly by helping the talks on Iran’s nuclear programme start much more quickly than previously agreed.

Iran says a deal on the temporary route through the strait of Hormuz has been agreed with Oman, describing it as a done deal, and is ready to register the details with the International Maritime Organisation.

Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, said he was waiting to hear a response from the Americans to the proposal. He added that he had consulted on the plan with China, which fully supported the proposal.

Saudi Arabia had been expected to endorse the Oman-Iran route through the strait last week, but pulled back partly due to anger that Iranian-backed Houthis had started attacking Saudi Arabia as part of their dispute over the future of Yemen.

Iran claims it has urged the Houthis to cease the attacks on Saudi Arabia but that it does not have control over Houthi decision-making.

Araghchi, speaking to reporters in New York, said: ‘We have introduced a plan to the US through the mediators that if certain conditions are met, the strait will be open within seven days and talks will start.’

He said the Iranian preconditions were not new, and were contained in the Islamabad memorandum of understanding that was signed by Trump.

The advantage of the proposal, apart from opening the strait and lifting the chokehold on the world economy, would be bringing the US to the talks on Iran’s nuclear programme much more quickly. Talks on the nuclear programme under the MoU would not have started for 60 days. Araghchi said he was staying in New York over the weekend to await an American response, but added he was not in a hurry.

Privately, Iranian officials believe they could reach a deal with the Americans, and the Saudi hurdle over aspects of the route could be overcome, but fear Israel will use its influence to pull the US president away from the proposal.

Araghchi added he would like the deal to go through before the midterm elections, by which he meant that the strait of Hormuz could be opened and energy prices thereby reduced, something Trump badly needs for the Republican party to survive a political mauling.

For the US, there are difficulties in the plan related to forcing Israel to end the war in Lebanon. Israel may object to giving Iran such clear control over the route through which ships would travel through the strait of Hormuz. Iran also wants to retain control of shipping to prevent some US military shipping going through the strait.

Issues such as whether tolls or navigational fees could be imposed by the littoral states Oman and Iran would be settled later in the process.

A faction inside Iran is arguing that Tehran should seek to escalate the conflict with a vulnerable US president, rather than let the crisis drift in its current deadlock. Brent crude was trading at about $107 (£81) a barrel on Thursday.

Some IRGC officers have also linked the strait of Hormuz issue to the closure of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway close to the south-west of Yemen now under control of Iranian-backed Houthis.

Maj Gen Rahim Safavi, a senior Iranian military figure, said: ‘If the Americans start a new war, a new front centred on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab strait may open before their eyes. Are they ready to enter the battle on this front? This is a question that they should pay more attention to.’

Domestically, Pezeshkian’s defiant message to the UN general assembly on Wednesday was deemed a success overall in that it balanced a refusal to bend the knee to ‘the US bully’ with a willingness to seek diplomatic talks.

He also proposed a new security architecture for the future in partnership with Gulf states, including those it has been bombarding in an effort to dislodge the US from its military bases.

Maj Gen Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the IRGC, praised Pezeshkian’s speech, saying: ‘We are not afraid of war. It is the loud and firm call of the Iranian nation – a call that resonated from the United Nations podium, through the words of the esteemed president, and reached the ears of the world.’
